audit.reasoning: Quote: confirmed verbatim in the now-downloaded Jacottet 1896 djvu text at Grammaire Soubiya p. 5 sect. 7 (record had no page locator; add it). The source also says accented vowels are long (p. 3 sect. 1), consistent with Bantu penultimate prominence, and the parallel Louyi sketch (p. 83 sect. 6) uses the same formula, so nothing internal contradicts the fixed: penultimate syllable coding. But the deciding source is a single 1896 missionary sketch with no tone analysis, no file was held before this reading, and Glottolog lists no grammar/phonology for Subiya; the two later sketches (Baumbach 1997, 145 pp with tone marking; Ndana et al. 2017 CASAS manual, 113 pp) are print-only and unexamined. No JIPA illustration, dissertation or instrumental study of Subiya prosody was found (CrossRef/OpenAlex; Hence 'thin': old second-tier source, no
audit.second_reader_evidence: ). Page header 'GRAMMAIRE SOUBIYA 5' at djvu line 1654, then '6° Accentuation, § 7. — Comme dans presque toutes les langues Bantou, l'accent tonique retombe en Soubiya sur la pénultième. Ex. : mu-kwáme [scanned mu-kwdme], homme; izûba, soleil, etc.' (lines 1656-1660), followed by the clitic-monosyllable and accented-monosyllabic-verb remarks (lines 1662-1669) exactly as the other first reader reports. So the record's source text is verbatim and the locator to add is 'Jacottet 1896, vol. 1, Grammaire Soubiya, 1re partie Phonétique

sources.quote: 'Comme dans presque toutes les langues Bantou, l'accent tonique retombe en Soubiya sur la penultieme. Ex. : mu-kwame, homme; izuba, soleil, etc. Les monosyllabes sont soit proclitiques, soit enclitiques ... Quelques verbes monosyllabiques ont cependant l'accent; ainsi : ba i, ils allerent; ba si ... D'autres ne l'ont pas ainsi ba ti'. Sect. 1: vowels 'breves quand elles ne sont pas accentuees; longues quand elles sont accentuees'.
